speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I worked in the police department for 16 years as a radio operator.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I heard that you met a lot of people from out of state.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yeah, I'm having some more tonight in California. Last year I had 92.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Wow.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah. This year I've only had 42 so far. Then you never know when they're coming.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do they just come by and look for you, or are these people that you met and you kept in touch with?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, they're strangers that come from California. I've never seen them before.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Are they people that you talked to while you were a police? No.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You see, Ray Bream called me up on the radio when I was working down there. He makes these cookie calls, you know, and asked me all about the town and everything. And I told him. And then that went over the air. So every week since that he calls me up from California, you know, and it goes over the air and these people hear him talking, and then they come up to see me. Oh. Yeah. So I don't know them. Oh, there's a few that, two or three that have come, you know, they came one time, then they've come back. But most of them, I don't know them. I've never seen them before.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you enjoy having people here like that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes, it's lots of fun.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yes. Sounds interesting.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, it is. Sometimes you're painting and sometimes you're washing because you can't be prepared for the company every minute, you know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have you had any jobs other than that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, I worked at the Union Legion Club for a while, for about ten years.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What did you do there?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Worked in the office.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Anything else? No. Interests, hobbies, and talents. You're an animal, right?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah. You mean what I like? I like people and animals.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Someone said, though, that people who treat animals well usually like people, too.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And so finally I couldn't stand her any longer. I took her out, took her and put her on the porch, and her hip was hurt. So I took her to the vet and he fixed her hip, put it in a cast, you know. And then every time I opened the door, Snooper, my dog, fell in love with the cat. And every time I opened the door, he'd push her in. So finally I got Snooper and I finally took the cat in. And I thought, well, I was feeding her so well and she was getting so fat. And one morning I woke up and had four kittens. But after the kittens got a little older, well, then I had her spayed. So now I knew I wouldn't have any more kittens. And I named her Tramp because that's what she was. And then a woman from California called me up and said, do you have any water in your house? And I said, yes. She said, well, get some. Well, I didn't know what she wanted. And finally she said, well, I have the water. And she said, now you named the cat Trampolina. So I did. So now her name's Trampolina.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Why didn't you just call and do that? Do you know? Pardon? Do you know why she called and...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, she didn't want me to just name her Tramp. Oh. She said if she... Snooper, get down. She said if she's a nice little cat, she says name her... And she is a good little cat. But, you know, I don't like cats very well.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, really?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But then you... What can you do? So anyway, I have Trampolina and she follows me all over. She's like a dog. When I take him for a walk, she's right there. Of course, she's a little bit lame, you know. She never did get over her injuries. But then she's a good cat. She's clean and she never gets... bothers anything in the kitchen or anything. And I guess as far as cats go, she's really a good one. But then...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, I like cats, but I'm allergic to them. If I'm around them a lot, you know, or the house has a lot of fur, you know, and I'm really here for quite a while, it will bother me. But otherwise, I'll pet cats and then I'll go wash my hands.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, that's the way with me. Well, anyway, she's... Like I say, she's a... far as cats... And you couldn't... Poor old thing has had such a hard life, you know. But she seems so grateful to have a home. But that's, I think, why she's so good. And of course, they romp and play, you know. And he just loves her. In fact, when she had her babies, he'd wait until she got out of the box, and then he'd crawl in and take care of the babies until she came back.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Ha ha ha ha ha! Yeah, that's unusual.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It is! Yes, it is. But he just loves Pampolina. He just loves her, you know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, brother.

words: BPW? Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And, um, Past Presidents Club. And Benefit Association. Let me see if I've bumped anything else. Senior Citizen Club. AARP. That's enough, isn't it?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, unless there's anything else that you think is important. Awards, honors, and ribbons. What? Awards, honors, and ribbons.

words: Well, I got a watch in the police department. And a citation from the governor.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What does that say? What's the citation for?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, it was for being a good citizen. Oh, and, uh... Oh, I... That's too many things to tell.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, if it's important to you, go ahead and tell it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well... I have a life membership in, uh, Parent Teachers.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And what kind of teachers?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Uh, PTA.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, you said Parent Teachers. How... That kind of seems unusual, since you don't have any children of your own. You just were interested as a person in the community? I see why you got the good citizenship award. Citation.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Because I was a... We started the PTA, you know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, you did?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, up in Warner. Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How did you meet your husband?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I went out to South Dakota, and he was out there, and I met him that way. Oh, yeah. I would visit my aunt. About two years. Oh, no. He just came back from visits. No, he didn't... He still lived in Dakota, you know. So then, uh, he came back, I don't know, four or five times, I think, and then we finally got married. But he was, uh... He got his back hurt in a mine, and he was an invalid for 32 years. So that was pretty rough.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How long had you been married before that happened?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, about... I don't remember all those dates.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, you know, not dates, just approximately, you know, whether it was ten years or three...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, no, it's about 20 years ago. 22 or something like that. That's been a long time ago. And then what else do you want to know?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Um, well, would you like to just kind of outline your life, or would you rather I just ask you various questions about... Ask questions?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, we weren't courting very much when he was out in Dakota, and I was in Illinois. Yes, we corresponded. Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Why did you decide to come out here, to Idaho?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, in the first place, he had bought a fruit acreage at Jellicle, and we moved out there. And then it didn't work out, so we came here. So that's the way it is.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What... Did he come here looking for a job in the mines, or were there just a lot of jobs?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, he came here to get a job in the mine. We weren't broke on the fruit farm. There wasn't any... Frosted every month of the year, and you couldn't raise fruit, so we got ripped on that outfit. So then we came here. And then we were here about four years, and then we went to Montana and homesteaded. And we were out there about eight years, and then we came back here. We've been here ever since.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you like homesteading in Montana?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It was fun. But I really would rather have a button to press and get lights than a kerosene lamp. Oh. Of course, it was... To me, it was just fun, you know. But it wasn't as easy as it is living in the city, you know. So then we came back here, and we sold the farm and came back here.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Were you glad to be going... Coming back to Kellogg?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, you bet. There's nowhere in the world I'd rather live. Why? Well, in the first place, it's beautiful country, and four seasons is what I love. Every spring and fall and winter with the... I love the snow. And the people here are wonderful, and that's all that matters.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you really have noticed a difference between your life in Chile and your life here?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, there isn't any comparison. Of course, then I was younger, too. You realize that. There's a difference in span of life, too, you know. But I know I've been back there, but I wouldn't want to... I could... I don't know how I ever lived there in the first place. Of course, I didn't know any better, but nights are hot, and it's smoky and dirty. No, not for me. I'm happy right here. It's the best place in all the world to live. I'm glad everybody don't know that, everybody be here. So you can keep it a secret.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, people tell us about the smelter smoke, so I think that keeps people away.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I think people get fed on smelter smoke. My heavens on earth, our kids here take like the kids, you know, that basketball and football. They're all supposed to be dying of lead poisoning, and they're winning everything in the state. That's a lot of hooey, that smelter smoke stuff. Well, I don't need that. If we have smelter smoke, so what? You know, there's nowhere in the world where it's perfect. Everything has a drawback, you know. It's either hot or cold or it rains too much or it don't rain enough. Well, here we have everything.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Or it's hot or there's snakes or something.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, and we don't have any snakes. That's one God blessing, isn't it?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I really find this pleasant.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, there ain't no better place in the world to live than here, I don't think. And the people are, they're like families. Now, all around here, our neighborhood, they've lived here for years, you know. Well, it is like the families. Like your very own, especially with me, I don't have any family, so my neighbors are my family.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Why did you have any children? Did you not want children or were you not able to?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I wasn't able to.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you want children originally?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, boy, and how. Well, I practically raised four. So, you know that I always wished someone would leave a baby on the doorstep, but they never did. They once left a little puppy in a basket, but then that wasn't a baby. But anyway, I kept the puppy.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Tell me about the four children you've always raised.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, they were, their mothers worked and was my cousin's kids, and so while she worked, I kept the kids in the daytime all the time, you know. And they're just like my own kids.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Now, there are people who are probably more interested in going back to where you came from.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I don't know. They've heard me laugh so much, I don't know if they ever want to listen anymore of it or not.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I've heard my grandmother a lot, and yet I really like her. Yeah. What do you think about mother's words?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I'll tell you what I think about it. If I had to live on bread and water, I would stay home and take care of my kids. Because in the first place, you take a mother that works all day, and she's, I've seen so much of it in the police department after all those years. And you take a mother that's working, and she works, and she's tired when she comes home. She can't adjust to her children. She's too tired. You know, you can only do so much. You put in a day's work, and then you have to come home and do another day's work. It's pretty hard on your nerves. So, if I had children, nobody would ever get me out of the house to eat and work. That's what I think about it. Did you give birth? Well, yes, I did, but when you have a husband that's in a wheelchair, you can't, they won't let you adopt the children. They, you know, they don't do that. So that's why I never adopted any. Now, what else do you want me to tell you?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When did you start working there, and was it financial, or did you just want to work?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, no, we spent all our money trying to cure my husband, you know. Took him all over trying to get him, see, arthritis set in after he was sick, when he got hurt. And after you'd go around here and there and everywhere trying to, you run out of money, you know, when you go so far. So that's why I worked in the police department, so I could earn enough money to keep us going.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you enjoy your job?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, boy, and how. Yes, I had enough, it was a wonderful job. And they were so nice to me there, you know. Yes, I did, I enjoyed every day I worked.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Before your husband was injured, were you ever apprehensive about his working in the mine?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I wasn't. It's safer to work in the mine than drive down the highway.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Someone else made that comment.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It is. No, I never worried about that. But then it was too bad he got hurt. But he was a very happy person, he never was depressed in any way. And he never had a doctor before in all his life, he was never sick. Poor old thing. But he took it on the chin when he knew, you know, that he wouldn't walk anymore, he was real. Well, he just figured it was his fate. So, he never, when he was sick, he never figured, you know, it was never a guru in me. So, and he used to play the violin. Yeah, he didn't, he never took any lessons, but anything he could sing, he could play, and he knew an awful lot of songs.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you play any musical instruments? TV.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's all.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What types of TV shows do you watch?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I love travelogues. And I like animal pictures, you know, and they have animal pictures. And like The Little House on the Prairie and stuff like that. And I like quiz shows. They're real good.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you like the ones that have been coming on recently, or do you keep changing it sometimes?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, well, there's some of them that I don't like. And there's one good thing about television, that you don't like it, you can turn it off. Or turn to another station. There's some of them, some programs I don't like very well. I don't like a lot of this crazy sex stuff they have now, I think that's better off in the bedroom or somewhere. And I don't like that. But they have many good other programs on, and Love the News and all that stuff, you know. But they have some real bad night programs. And I like that. I like that awful well. And what else do you want me to tell you?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, I've got lots of questions, as long as you'll keep answering them. If you get tired, you can send me away. But I have quite a few questions. What types of magazines and newspapers do you subscribe to regularly?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I get the Kellogg Evening News and the, and the Volcan paper, the review. And I get the Reader's Digest and TV Guide. That's the kind of magazines I like. All those others you buy, but then, you know, I don't take them.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You buy occasional.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, that's right.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you like to read?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, you bet.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What types of books do you read?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I like to read religious books a lot. You know, there's some of them that are very good. And I like to read those kind of books. And Mystery Magazine, or Mystery, yes, it works in print. I like Mystery. But I don't like old, the books they have nowadays, I don't want to read them. The kind they have now in, you know, some of the best sellers, I think they ought to have them, but the poor sellers, as far as I'm concerned. Yeah, I think you should read them. They're good. But then everybody has their own taste, whatever they like. And like I say, if they have all kinds of books, you buy what you want. And everybody has a different idea of what they want to read, and that's what they can read. But these new ones, uh-uh. There's too many, I'd rather go out and look at some flowers or a tree or something, something that's beautiful, besides a lot of dirty words in a book. That's true.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you like to go camping?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, you bet. And I like to fish. I don't catch very many, but it's a lot of fun down on the hook in the water.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is there any type of fish you like the best?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, when we were kids, my dad used to take us out in the rivers then, and we used to get bullheads. But now, of course, out here mostly you get trout.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And... You like those?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, uh, to... you mean to eat?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yes, to eat.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I don't know, I can't remember what a bullhead tastes like, because it's been so many years ago, but trout's very good.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: There's also a lot of eaters and catfish.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh yeah, well, no, when we were back there, we had a... we had a... my dad... we had a pole, and we had a string and a cork. And when the cork went under the water, you just sat there. Well, then you had a fish. But now you wave the strings.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, I mean as far as cleaning them.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, oh yes, gee, those other things are awful hard. I think out here they call them catfish. They're on that order anyway.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, but they call them bullheads. I'm used to calling them catfish.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, and you have to skin them. So they're hard to clean. But trout really is an awful good fish.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you hunt? Do you have any hunters?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, never. I wouldn't shoot anything. No. Uh-uh. I don't even like to eat wild meat, because the poor little deer, you think about them when you're eating the meat.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And what about the poor little cow?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I don't know, I guess you're used to that. Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I used to want to catch catfish.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But if I ever saw a cow being shot or killed, I couldn't eat it. But when you buy it in the butcher shop, you don't think that, you know. Yeah. It was a funny thing the other day, a woman was telling me that they raised some, or did I hear it on the radio? I don't know. But anyways, they raised ducks. And they, no, she's telling me it was in California. And they raised ducks. And she said then they killed the ducks, you know, and they had them all named. And then when they put them in the freezer, they cleaned them and put them in the freezer and put the names on each one. And nobody could eat them. So they had to give the ducks away. It was a crazy thing to put the names on, wasn't it? I know. That's what she said, too.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah. If I got attached to an animal, it would really make it hard.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, you couldn't. No.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did the Depression have much effect on your life? No.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We lived here and everybody worked. They maybe worked four days a week or so, you know. But food was cheaper and everybody got along fine. Back east, I knew there was a Depression because I went back there that one time and it was terrible. Nobody was working or anything. But in our country here, everybody that wanted to work could work, you know, maybe four days a week. Well, that would keep you going at least.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, did they work four days a week so that more people could work? Yes. I wonder if people are still going to do that sort of thing now. I don't think it is yet, but I've heard of other places kind of being willing to take a little risk themselves so that other people can have a go.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I don't know. I think if it came right down to it, they would. I don't know everywhere, but I think they would here because people are awful good here about things. Of course, I always brag about this place because I love it. You know, when you like anything, it's easy to... And I don't... It is that people here are so darn good. You know, if you have any trouble or anything, that's when you find out how good people are. And I know from working where I did down at the police department that anybody get in trouble and everybody gets in. Everybody. Well, they don't do that in a bigger town, you know. Well, in the first place, everybody knows everybody. And when you have that terrible mine disaster up here at the Sunshine Mines, you can't imagine how the whole town mourned. It was terrible.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I heard that the town really got together. I heard that it just... everybody really pulled together.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, they did. Well, everybody... If you didn't have anybody in the mine, you knew somebody that did have. You know, that many people you would, you know. So everybody had a heartache.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How long did it really take for Kellogg to recover from that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I never... I don't think they recovered yet. I don't think so. You mean the memory or what?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I just mean, you know, before people started... I think that was a really bad question. You know, just before things seemed to get back flowing again.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Back to normal. Yeah. Well, I don't know. I would think... Before the hurt quit coming, I would think, you know, for the outsiders, you know. Of course, people... their own people never forget it. But outsiders, you know, you... The time goes on while, you know, it gets a little easier. But I would think it was six months before really everybody, the outsiders did... Well, like when you went to the store, when we had that disaster, nobody asked you if you wanted a cup of coffee or... It really carried on conversation. Everybody was sick. But then gradually it worked back to where people were normal again.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Mm-hmm. Um... What were some of the things that you and your brothers and sisters did for recreation when you were growing up? Well...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Of course, I lived in the city. And the only thing we ever done is go to parks and stuff like that. I never saw a cow till I was 12 years old.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, really?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, we lived where there was zoos, but they never had cows in zoos, you know. So, first cow I ever saw, I thought all cows done live for was to horn ya. You know, that's what I thought. Well, I would face any kind of an animal than a cow because, you know, we got used to the other animals, but a cow, you know, you never... They didn't have cows in cities. So, we just were normal kids and played games and went swimming and stuff like that, you know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you go camping or were you...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, my dad took every summer he'd take us two weeks camping along the DuPage River.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is that in Illinois? Yeah. Did you go outside of Illinois very much when you were growing up?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, we used to go to Michigan and Indiana and stuff like that. There was no... Not like now with a lot of cars, you know. But we'd go on like excursions and stuff, you know, like go over to Lake Michigan, go to Chicago, and we weren't only a few miles from Chicago. And then we would go on the boat, you know, Benton Harbor and places like that, Michigan City and Milwaukee and stuff like that. That's what we'd do in the summer, you know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You like to travel, right?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes, I like to travel.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When you travel, do you like to go see people or places?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, it all depends on now I'm going to California the 9th down to San Diego, and I'm going to go down, and I'm not going to do anything but... Paul, one of the kids that I practically raised, and I'm just going to play with the three kids, and they can go anywhere they want to, but I'm going to visit the kids. That's the truth. But I like to go and see things, too, you know. But I've been to Hawaii and...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How did you like Hawaii?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, we were there six weeks, and it was very beautiful, you know. Of course, the flowers and everything, you know, well, they grow like mad. And it was very, very beautiful, but I think if I had to live there, I wouldn't like it because it's all the same all the time. You know, you don't see no snow, or you don't see the colors in the forest, or the fall, and that's what I like.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have you involved yourself with winter sports?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, not here. Well, years ago, we used to go skiing before they had ski lodges. We used to ski up here in the dumps, you know, mine dumps. But then now I don't ski anymore. I'm lucky if I walk around pretty good.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Were you interested, when you were a Joliet, were you interested in learning how to ski?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, we never had no skiing back there. Gee, no.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I mean, when I was little, I read books, and people, you know, talked about people skiing, and always thought it would be really neat to learn how to ski.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I never read a book or any... I didn't know there was any skiing until I came out where there was much snow. Because there, it's level. And when it snows back there, now, we have the big, fat flakes that come down there, they're beautiful. But there, it's more like a sleet. And it's very cold in the winter. I used to go, I went to the convent when I was a little girl, and I used to have to walk. We didn't have buses those days, you know. And you used to have to take the streetcar in the morning, and then get off, then walk about four blocks to the convent every day, you know. And, gee, you'd get stingers in your hands and your legs getting a couple of blocks sometimes. It was real cold. But here, we don't have that bad cold weather. And there, it was damp, more damp, too, you know. But we just had a lot of fun. Like all kids, we played games and baseball and stuff like that, you know. And we did a lot of skating in the winter. I remember my father bought me skates, and they were two runners when I was little. And he used to take me skating, and the kids made fun of me because I had two runners on my skates. Boy, was I unhappy, and I was glad when I got my first one with one blade on it, you know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Were two runners unusual?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I was very small, and my dad thought they'd be better, you know, than one. No, some, there wasn't very many that ever had two that I can remember, because I was littler than a lot of them that had skates, too.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, but it sounds like something like a training bike, you know.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, that's the same, it's the same idea as a training bike.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I wouldn't mind doing that with two runners, not having your skates in my life. I wouldn't mind starting out on two runners, but I can see people kidding you about it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, when you, you know, kids are kind of cruel sometimes, you know. They say, what are you skating with those on, you know, and get her a basket and put her in the basket and all that stuff. But anyway, my dad took me and went by the hand and we went skating. We used to skate then on the rivers, they used to freeze over. They don't do that anymore. Why? Well, the climate's changing so many times everywhere. We used to never have any wind out here. I used to be so happy when I'd see a little wind so I could wash blankets. And now I'm, when I see the wind, I'm afraid to put them on there, I fear they'll blow off. That's the difference in the climate. It really has changed a lot since we've been here.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I've always been amazed at the idea of putting something out to dry and it takes an hour here and in Georgia it always took two or three, you know.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Where did you live in Georgia? Columbus. I was down at Brunswick. You know where that is?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I haven't been there, but I know where it is.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It's near the Florida line. I was down there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was that a visit or? Yeah. How did you like it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, it was, to me, I thought it was, I liked to see the trees with all the stuff hanging down like we see in the horror movies, you know, and stuff. And it was, to me, it was, of course it was a flat country and I liked the mountains. But we went down as far, we went down into Florida and it was a pretty country, you know, only there were so many snakes. Yeah. See?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I'm going to give you a cup of coffee.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Would you like a cup of coffee?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, would you?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah. Let me get some. Here, I'll get it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did, were you affected pretty much by the war? What caused World War II?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, in the World War, my brother went to the war, but he never got across the waters.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: World War II?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: World War I.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: World War I.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He was only 17 and he was in the camp when they signed, the armistice was signed, you know, so he never got to go. And he was the only one, my sister was already dead and my brother was my heart child. And I just loved him. But he didn't go because he died later on of penicillin. Yeah. He was only married a year.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So that's what he was in need of and he just not, was he too far away from the doctor or?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, but they didn't have all this penicillin those days either. You know, and you, now they have everything, but peritonitis said in those days, well, you was a goner. And that's what happened to him. No, he went to the doctor the night before he took sick. In the afternoon they operated on him that night. He lived two days.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: He lived two days? Yeah. I bet you were relieved though that he didn't have to go overseas during the war.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, he wanted to go so bad that I kind of felt sorry for him. You know, he was in camp in Georgia when the war ended.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When was he in Georgia? Do you remember?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I don't remember.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What were some of the things that you did right after your husband got married for recreation?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, we went, we danced a lot. He used to play for dances. And we danced a lot. He didn't dance much. He'd done the playing and I'd done the dancing. And just, we just had friends in and, you know, like people live nowadays. So.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What do you think are the major differences between when you were growing up and now? With children growing up?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, it's kind of, it's like two different lives. Now, when we were kids, we were contended to be home. Home was the nicest place in the world. You know, in our own home. And nowadays, kids don't want to be home. They have to have recreations of all kinds. We didn't have anything like that. We were happy. We'd go sleigh riding in the winter and skating and stuff. You know, we didn't have to have clubs to go to or nothing like they do now. Of course, I think a lot of that is because they don't have no home life. And my mother was a wonderful person and made our life every minute of every hour happy. And now I've got so many things to be thankful for.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did your mother can and preserve foods?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. Uh-uh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have you ever done that sort of thing?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes. I used to can everything. But nowadays, by the time you buy the jars and the sugar and the fruit, they have to ship everything in. It's cheaper to buy a can. Maybe it isn't as good. Maybe it's better than what I canned. I don't know. But for me now, I don't do anything like that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I bought some peaches and canos and I decided that it wasn't worth the effort. And they weren't just fresh off the trees?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They're not.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: They're Yakima. Yeah. So what's out of my garden makes sense, but the other things don't make sense.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, if a person, if you have to buy it in the first place, they don't pay. But those early garden peaches are wonderful peaches and that's what I buy. You know, stuff like that. Come on, baby doll. What else do you want to know?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have you been involved in the church at Kittenden?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes. I used to teach Sunday school.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What church was it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: The United Church. I used to teach, but then after I started to work, I couldn't take care of the house and Korty and I had to sleep sometimes, you know. So I didn't go in the mornings anymore.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Does church still play and they just want you to go?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I'm sorry to say it, I don't go very much. I listen to the programs on the radio on Sunday mornings. That maybe isn't the best thing to do, but it's the easiest. So that's...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You are involved then, at least with listening.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, you bet. And I love to read books like, you know, Bible story books and stuff like that. I like that. And that, but then, I don't know, I worked so many years and you just kind of get out of the habit of going to church. Although I donate to the church. I always donate to the church, but I'm not a very good church member.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was your husband also involved?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, no. Well, no, he wasn't. He never, well, I don't know. I usually went to church and he stayed home and done the dishes. So maybe I didn't coach him to go because I knew if I'd come home I'd have to wash the dishes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you have animals?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, always. I always had dogs. But this is the first cat. But I always had dogs. Then when they die, I die a little bit too.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, they really become a part of your life. I mean, when children talk about their children, and people with animals wind up talking about their animals quite frequently. Are there any interesting incidents that you can think about that happened when you were working at the police department?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, no, lots of them. But then I guess maybe you'd better not tell all that stuff. Well, we had one little boy, he used to, he'd always bring them to the station because he was shoplifting, you know. So one day when they brought him in, I told him, I said, I didn't have any little boys. Of course, they used to bring the kids in and we'd talk to them, you know. Because we could do more with them than the police. They were frightened of the police, you know. So I told him, I said, I said, Dillinger started out like that. And he would take a little and more and pretty soon he got to be terrible. He said, was he your brother? And I said, no, he wasn't in any relation, thank heavens. But I told him if he wanted anything to come and ask me for the money and he could buy it, you know. So he did that for about four years. When he wanted anything, he'd come in and I'd give it, and we never had him back anymore. No, no, just little things. He was only six years old. And he'd like a little car maybe or candy bar or something like that, you know. And I always kept cookies down at the police department so whenever they'd come in, you know, give them a cookie or a lollipop or something. Because they'd bring little children in sometimes and they were real frightened. And you'd be surprised what a candy bar or what a cookie or lollipop would do for the kids, you know. Or maybe... Well, lots of times the mother would have to come on account of the father. And the little things would be waiting up, our jails were downstairs. Well, they'd let the little children sit upstairs with me, you know. Well, give them a cookie or something, kind of calm them down, feel sorry for them, you know. And that's the kind of stuff we used to do. Or if a man and woman come in and were having a terrible time, you'd give them each a cup of coffee, they'd sit them down, you know. Maybe they'd make up a little bit. Tricks and all trades, isn't there? Well, you know, they're all people. You know, it's... They're... Everybody's human, you know. And it's so much easier to be nice to people than be mean to them. It's awful hard to be mean to anybody, but it's so easy to be nice. And that's where I figured a cup of coffee would... I know the chief told me one time, he said, we sure would get a lot more fines if you weren't around because there's people who'd come in and we'd put them in jail, not only for having a fight, but if they'd get a cup of coffee and make up, well, we'd lose our fine. But I guess we prospered anyway. Radio operator. Radio operators. Then we done the filing and made out accident reports, helped them with accident reports. We done everything, but you have little things, you know. And we made out the complaints and the warrants and stuff like that. And then we had to take care of the women, which we'd have to search the women, you know, when they brought them in. And take care of the women too, you know, if they hollered for something while we went down the men. The police took care of the men, and we took care... But we didn't have very many women in once in a great while. And there's a room you'd have the same ones in, so you'd get well acquainted with them, you know. And then you know what they wanted.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What were women used to buy at the bar?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, mostly for being drunk, you know. And then, oh, sometimes we had one woman, and she used to, if anybody put any money on the bar, she'd grab it. And then we'd have to search her, you know, and get the money back. She'd have it maybe in her shoe or somewhere. But we had to take care of the women. But then they weren't bad to take care of. They were all reasonable, you know. Mostly they'd go to sleep, and when they'd wake up, they'd be sorry. And like I say, we never had anything. We had two different times, murder times, but they came in and told me. One fellow shot a man, and he come in and told me that he did, and I told him to stay there until the police come, and he did.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was it an accident? No. No.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He was a—this other man was kind of trying to get his wife, I guess, and so he come in one day, and Boyd was cleaning fish, and they'd been fishing, and he told him to stay out, and he didn't do it, so he just let him have it. And the other man, he was kind of a pitiful thing, and he was in a room in the boarding house, and they were teasing him all the time about him having a lot of money and everything, you know. And so they kept on and on until they had the poor man almost crazy, so they thought they were breaking in, and he shot one of them, and he come up and told me.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It doesn't sound like he would be frightened in those circumstances.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No! No, they wouldn't.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: He wouldn't just kill somebody just, you know, out on the street.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, they wouldn't hurt me. No, I never was afraid of any of them. There was never one man that they brought in that I ever heard even cuss. You know, they'd look over and see that there was—see our—the radio was like over here, and then—well, you've been in the police department, haven't you?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Not here.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, we had the radio was like over there, and then there's a counter, and then this is all open here, and then the jails are downstairs. And they'd be on the other side of the counter, and if they happened to look—say something not nice, they'd look over, and half of them would say, excuse me. And there were even gentlemen when they were drunk, most of them. At least I thought there were. No, no.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: He wants an attention, doesn't he?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, he wants to go for a walk. Oh. I take him up the trail here in Trampoline every day.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, you mean up through here somewhere?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Up the back hill. Oh. It's old Haystack Peak out here. And—oh, he heard me say that. Ha, ha, ha. He can even—he even knows when you spell stuff.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, yeah. Doctors, they're really smart. It's amazing how smart they really are.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, is there anything else you want to know?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Are there any more stories you'd like to tell me?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I don't think I know very many. The only thing I can say that the town has changed, when we first came here, there wasn't any pavements or anything, you know. And you used to come down the hill and mud, oh, mud, mud, downtown. You know, they used to lay planks down for you to walk on, you know, downtown. It was awful muddy. So I see many, many changes since I've been here. And I know when they paved the street, finally put paving on the street to dance for two nights in the street. They had a band. And then one thing I think is kind of cute, we had a strike here, you know, and it lasted quite a while. And they decided to paint the town. So everybody got in and they painted the town. You know, the women and the kids and everybody painted. And then when they, then the first night they had great big tables in front of, blocked off the street in front of the police department. And they had hot dogs and buns and baked beans and potato salad and everybody come to eat. And then the next night they had the dance for everybody painting, you know. See, the merchants furnished all that stuff for them painting. They painted everything. We just had a beautiful town.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was they just decided while they weren't working that they would just improve the town?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, so they did.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, that's marvelous. Yeah. You know, I'm just amazed. People don't tend to do those sorts of things anymore.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, they didn't. It was funny. The little kids would come in for paint brushes. We had them at the police department, you know. Boy, little things would come in. You couldn't, I think they had about a quart of paint on them and about a pint on the building. But they were real cute. And they worked hard, you know. Of course, the little kids, they gave everybody paintbrush, you know. Some of the women had pictures that took, that was on television, showed some pictures. And there was one big, oh, she was a pretty big fat woman and she was up on the ladder just to paint to beat the band. And she got kind of mad because she didn't know they took her picture. Oh. But they did that, and I think that was a nice thing to tell.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, it shows a lot of community spirit.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, it is. And like I say, if you have any trouble in this town, boy, everybody pitches in and helps.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Mm-hmm. Are there any changes in the town?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think it gets better and better. It never gets worse and worse.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You sound like a very positive person, and it's really nice to meet positive people.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I think that's true. They've improved the town so much and done so many things since I came. You wouldn't know it was the same place. We've got the nicest swimming pool and we've got a little park and a nice ballground. And they've done everything they could to make people happy, and that's all you can do. No, I, and we've got good supermarkets, just wonderful supermarkets, you know. And what more could you do? You know, maybe in a big city they have old museums and stuff like that. But museums are fine, but friends are what count. You know, you get tired of going to a museum. You never get tired of friends. So that's the way I feel about the town. They've improved it. I've never seen anything that they've gone backward. They've gone forward all the time. And we've got a good highway now, where we used to go around the Fourth of July around all the curbs and I'd get sick and heave. Well, now it's straight and a good road. What more could you ask?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, it's really nice to get on that road.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, it is. And like in California where they have all those highways, my goodness, I don't know how people drive. And like here in a small town, now like in California, I was down there a couple years ago, we wanted to go anywhere. We rode and rode for hours to get anyplace. So if you have friends living down there, you don't go and see them because it takes so long to get there. And here you can get in the car and jump, go down the hill and you're right where you want to be.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, we've enjoyed when we came here the other time, and this time that some of us walked back to the motel from where we were and there were a lot of people that we went to see that we could walk to where we were staying from there. So there wasn't any hassle at all with just having one car.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's right. And we've got wonderful schools. And on the hospital it's the right to be sick in because the nurses over there are like your family. They don't give you a number like they do in big cities. You're really a person. And that's something.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You mentioned starting the PTA. Was it you and a group of people?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, we were charter members. There's only three of us left.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Why did you get involved with the school?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I always figured that I didn't have any children and I had more time than people that did. Now that's the way I figured it. You know, I had those days I didn't work and I had all day, and people that have children, they have to feed them and take care of them and everything, and they don't have as much time as I had. So I just figured it was up to me to do that. And that's how I got involved. So anyway, we don't have our school up here anymore. They bust the kids now.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, down in Tequilla. Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I guess it was a better way to be because it costs an awful lot to keep up a school and we didn't have too terrible many children up here, you know. Of course, you hate to see the school go, you know, and it was a dandy school. And they took them to schools that weren't quite so nice, but then I guess they, in order to cut down on taxes and stuff, they have to do what they see fit. So our children, they meet right out here in the driveway and they pick them up and take them.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you think that's changed people's involvement with the school, not having it right in the area and having it down in Kellogg, or is it just close enough in Kellogg?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, now I can understand in a big city where they bust them miles, you know, and have a school close. Now my cousin's little girl, she lives over there, and they have a school three blocks. And those children have to go about four miles to go to another school. That, I think, is ridiculous. But like here where it's close, it don't take the children but a few minutes to go down to Kellogg, and it's all one anyway. Why, I think that it makes a lot of difference. It depends on where you live. But I know if I was living, if I had three little boys and lived a couple of blocks from the school, and then I had to get up early in the morning, you'd get the kids ready to bust some way over across the city. I wouldn't like that. But like here, I think it's okay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I wasn't sure exactly how far away Portner is. You know, it's like the same town.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, this is the old town. You see, when they discovered ore, they discovered it right up here a little ways. And then they later on figured they would tunnel in and get the ore. And that's what built Kellogg. So then that's why we're really all in one. Yes, right up the gulfs here. You haven't been up to the ski lodge, have you?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, I haven't.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, when you get up there, you turn off to the left, and it was right up there where they discovered the ore. Well, then they, you know, they used to have the cable go across. Of course, I wasn't here then. I only know what I'm, what I've heard people say. And then they, and it was all houses all up the gulf and all over. But then when they decided that they would tunnel in, then they went down, they started, and that's what started Kellogg. Well, then of course, there was more flat land in Kellogg than there was up here, as you can see. Because there was houses, many of them are gone now. They burned them down because people would go away, and they'd go to Rack and Rune, and so they burned many of them down.
